title: Why small‑boat crossings fell: Border Security Command’s approach and remaining risks
label: 21 October 2026 · Border Security Command oral evidence
summary: The Border Security Command (BSC) and National Crime Agency (NCA) told MPs that small‑boat arrivals to the UK fell by about half this year because of coordinated enforcement, international disruption of supply chains and upstream work with partner countries. They described how BSC coordinates agencies, where it still needs to improve, the role of intelligence and Europe, recent difficult landings on the south coast, and how deterrence, returns and safe/legal routes fit into future policy. They warned displacement and large boats remain serious risks.

chapters.title: Why crossings have fallen
chapters.takeaway: Border Security Command and the NCA say improved, coordinated enforcement—especially hitting equipment and facilitators—and upstream work with partners explain most of the roughly 50% fall in boats this year.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want to know whether the drop in small‑boat arrivals is down to policy and enforcement, or just luck.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Arrivals are much lower: about 16,000 fewer people and around 305 boats so far this year, roughly half the boats from this time last year.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: BSC was created to bring together enforcement, intelligence and international work. We focus on reducing pull factors, disrupting supply chains, and working with near‑border partners—principally France.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: The NCA made this a main effort. We run about 100 operations at any time against social media, equipment suppliers, high‑value targets, criminal finances and the key actors in northern France.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: Key indicators we track include seizures of boats and engines, operational disruptions overseas and arrests—sometimes disruption without arrest is more effective at stopping crossings.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Why now? These measures have been talked about for years—what changed to produce the fall?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: It takes time to bed in: relationships, training and resourcing across agencies and with partners have come together this year, and upstream work is bearing fruit.

chapters.title: How BSC coordinates agencies and measures success
chapters.takeaway: BSC acts as a system leader, funding and directing work across agencies; they monitor many measures—not just crossings—to decide what to keep, scale up or change.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Has inter‑agency co‑operation improved since BSC was set up? Anything still missing?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Yes—two years in, relationships and systems are much better. BSC brought maritime, small‑boats, and Home Office intelligence together, giving a clearer operational focus.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: But success doesn’t mean complacency: even if arrivals fall below 25,000 it’s still too many and we keep pushing.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: Some areas—criminal finance, cash economies and informal money transfer (hawaladars)—are harder and need more priority, because they underpin the facilitation business model.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: How do you judge value for money and what would you spend extra funding on?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: BSC channels funding across Home Office, NCA and partners and runs a dynamic board to assess impact. We’ll double down on things that work—especially upstream disruption and tackling pull factors.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: We apply tactics used against national security threats; as we evaluate what works, we redeploy resources. Upstream work and following the money are high‑value areas but difficult.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Has anything been stopped as not value for money?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Not yet—BSC is still early in its first full cycle. Some programmes are being refocused to target organised immigration crime more precisely rather than broader criminality.

chapters.title: Intelligence, Europe and upstream disruption
chapters.takeaway: The NCA and BSC emphasise intelligence‑led work, joint operations in Europe, and taskforces that tackle routes and source countries well before migrants reach France.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: Can intelligence be improved further, especially if instability grows in other countries?

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: We aim for maximum coverage—NCA has a well‑resourced intelligence effort, strong EU liaison via Europol and more joint investigations and international liaison officers than before.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Home Office intelligence is now embedded in BSC. We run taskforces across three main routes—north‑east Africa/central Mediterranean; the Iraq/Turkey/Syria route; and western Europe/Balkans—so we can track journeys and facilitators across borders.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Would rejoining Eurodac help?

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: Yes—more real‑time biometric and asylum data from Europe would improve identification and our ability to stop repeated claims or detect people who passed through other countries.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: How do you ensure money sent to partner countries is used properly?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: We work through FCDO channels and their assurance processes. There is a pragmatic balance: some partner states have difficult records, but we must work with them while upholding legal standards.

chapters.title: Operations at sea, rescues and the south‑coast incidents
chapters.takeaway: Most rescues are done by BSC’s vessels; the south‑coast landings in September exposed risks from long crossings, violent local protests and the need for better local contingencies and communications.

turns.speaker: Margaret Mullane
turns.text: What worries you most now about organised crime adapting?

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: They adapt, but their model is vulnerable: it needs boats, engines, logistics and timing. We’ve increased their costs and risk so they’re changing tactics; we’re trying to stay ahead.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: I worry about bigger boats and higher occupancies: we had a 230‑person boat and rescues of 168 on one launch. A major casualty is sadly possible if we’re not careful.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: There were launches from Normandy and Dieppe this year as gangs tried to displace away from Calais/Dunkirk. That required fast co‑ordination with French, Belgian and Dutch partners and local UK police.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How are migrants moving from northern camps to these western launch points?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Often by van or public transport; the train ride from Paris can take many hours. French authorities are alert to prevent the north camps model repeating in the west.

turns.speaker: Mr Paul Kohler
turns.text: Tell us about the south‑coast landings and the RNLI role—why were they involved?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Most rescues (about 98%) are handled by BSC assets and modified crew transfer vessels. But some landings were far from our usual patrol area; the RNLI responded where the coastguard tasked them.

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: After the first unexpected arrival, protesters interfered at a marina, creating public‑order and safeguarding problems. For another landing we transferred people to a Border Security vessel and sent them to Dover; later arrivals needed police protection onshore.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: What contingency changes have you made so RNLI aren’t the default responders?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: We’ve put additional contingency plans in place, are procuring more crew transfer vessels, and will position assets so we can respond without routinely involving RNLI except where they are best placed.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: How long were those migrants at sea?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Roughly 30–40 hours in one case. Crossing long distances in winter would raise the risk of deaths—so shutting routes down is urgent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Were the southern landings detected late?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: They were detected but too late to intercept at sea on a very busy day. Those two events were under 0.1% of recent arrivals, but they exposed gaps we’ve addressed.

turns.speaker: Margaret Mullane
turns.text: Are people who arrived in those incidents being security‑checked?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Yes—everybody who arrives enters biometric and debrief processes. Small‑boat arrivals are photographed, fingerprinted and interviewed; most people comply and want to claim asylum.

chapters.title: Returns, deterrence and the policy mix
chapters.takeaway: BSC and NCA favour a mix: upstream prevention, communications to counter lies sold by gangs, targeted returns and safe/legal routes; enforcement and consequences for illegal work are central to deterrence.

turns.speaker: Mr Paul Kohler
turns.text: Was Operation Hillmore (the France returns pilot) a success and why did it end?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: It returned about 1,631 people and discouraged many others: UNHCR processed around 10,000 applications through the scheme. It was always a year‑long pilot; France wanted EU‑level arrangements instead of a bilateral extension.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: Quick, reliable returns remove incentives for OCGs and undermine their message that crossing is easy and consequence‑free.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do safe and legal routes have a role?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Yes—if they let genuine asylum seekers apply safely and stop people taking dangerous journeys. The Hillmore pilot showed safe routes can be a deterrent as well as a humanitarian route.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: How do you identify people with no documents and check if they’re a risk?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Debriefing at Manston, biometric checks and embedded counter‑terror officers help. Most small‑boat arrivals are identified and enrolled biometrically, and the intelligence picture is improving.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: We want Eurodac‑style sharing and more European data to reduce blind spots—real‑time biometric alerts help spot repeat routes or criminal links.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about consequences for working illegally or breaking asylum rules?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: Consequences matter for deterrence. We’re increasing work to stop illegal employment—such enforcement undermines the pull factor that gangs exploit.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point: are you confident the gains will hold?

turns.speaker: Duncan Capps
turns.text: We’ve reduced crossings significantly but risks remain: displacement, larger boats and the winter. We must keep pressure on all parts of the criminal model and on communications in source countries.

turns.speaker: Rob Jones
turns.text: We’re disrupting gangs and following leads across Europe and upstream. The business model is under strain—our job is to keep it that way until it’s no longer viable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. The Committee appreciates the work and the clear explanation of risks and next steps.
